Answer: This uses only basic Regex knowledge to provide regex for extracting just Yes and No in your text. We are using positive lookahead assertions as you know. In the Regex pattern, we create groups which we will call later to extract the matching values.

So, in my solution, I've extracted few regex groups
\begin{itemize}
\item `1.Yes` group for the clause which starts Yes
\item `Clause` which starts the clause with text you give
\item and few extra groups like "No" which match only  No clause
\end{itemize}

Now, what I did, I searched "Yes" in any location and used Regex `yes.Regex(clause.group(1)) // will give me clause"yes"`

\begin{code}
(?:\s*Yes\s+)(.*)
\end{code}

[Online demo here](https://regex101.com/r/K5bwWn/1)

If it is not a Yes start (which is not a Yes), it will be match in second `.*` group.

To search any Yes in my above regex pattern, the Regex can use (the `.*` would also capture, but for clarity purpose, I've extracted it out) like this

\begin{code}
Yes .*
\end{code}

See also: [online demo here](https://regex101.com/r/K5bwWn/2)

# Exercises for Lesson 40 -- Aggregation (Section 5-6C(i) of the Model)
The aggregation principle allows a limited partnership to elect that a portfolio of partnerships treated as partnerships for federal tax purposes be treated as a single taxable entity. Partners in these multiple partner entities that are treated as partnerships for federal tax purposes must have the same tax classifications for federal income tax purposes. One partner classification, however, cannot be used to "stuff" any specific partnership or multiple partnership interests within any one partnership. Each partnership that may exercise the aggregation election must follow each of the aggregation partnership principles set out in Notice 88-77.
In 2012, Xyumax formed a single-member limited partnership, the Xyumax Opco, and a single-member limited liability company ("Xyumax HoldCo"). Both entities would be treated as partnerships for federal tax purposes unless their activities fell within one of the limited exceptions to partnership classification.[237] Because Xyumax wanted each limited partnership and limited liability company treated as a partnership for federal tax purposes unless otherwise required under Section 1212, Xyumax elected to form a series of ten partnerships,[238] each organized as a Delaware limited liability partnership ("Delaware Partnership") and each having the same tax identification number and having substantially common and identically worded agreements with Xyumax. Xyumax had identical capital account balances in each of the ten Delaware Partnerships.[239] Under all of the arrangements, a ten-digit capital account number designated “XXY” was placed on the top of every capital account in each Delaware Partnership. This same ten-digit capital account number was also put at the beginning of each general partnership agreement. The agreements between Xyumax and each partnership provided for management functions, such as accounting, payroll and filing tax returns, to be provided by, or through agreements with, the Xyumax Opco, which was organized and operated to do the same thing. As a limited partnership, the Xyumax Opco itself did not engage in any activity as a partnership, and no interest held by an Xyumax-affiliated Delaware Partnership was deemed to result in Xyumax-affiliated capital. Xyumax had the identical assets, interests or profits held by ten similar partnerships organized under New York law as limited liability partnerships. As a consequence of being organized as limited liability partnerships, each limited liability partnership filed separate federal, state, and local income tax returns.[240]  The Series was a separate segment from the Opco as separate accounting entries for Xyumax HoldCo's business were maintained.[241] When these limited liability companies were aggregated, the result was that the same tax identification number was used both as a partnership for tax reporting purposes and as a single member limited liability partnership for federal income tax filing purposes.[242] After filing the aggregation election (for both entities), the taxpayer maintained the same organizational structure and tax treatment after the aggregation election was filed to minimize recordkeeping, paperwork and legal/ tax costs.[243]
After an examination of Xyumax by Internal Revenue Service, Xyumax sought an opinion and a determination on whether Xyumax and Xyumax HoldCo satisfied the aggregation rules.[244] The Tax Court first addressed whether the two-member aggregation rule in Treas. Reg. § 1.1212-3(c) applied.[245] Relying on the Ninth Circuit’s “two-owner rule,”[246] the court held that, because only two member organizations elected to aggregate their multiple partner entities into a single partnership that would be treated as a partnership for federal tax purposes in all taxing years, the aggregation regime of Regulation Section 1.1212-3(c) did not apply.[247] Accordingly, Internal Revenue did not have to prove that any of the Delaware partnerships were separate entities. Therefore, the Court concluded that in every tax year the two aggregate partnership were not treated as separate entities[248]
